01a0ff11-5a79-51fe-9d67-b88a19db896c.name: Roman Catholic Parish Church and Monastery of St. Ignatius of Loyola
01a0ff11-5a79-51fe-9d67-b88a19db896c.alternate_name: Jesuit Church and Monastery of Győr
01a0ff11-5a79-51fe-9d67-b88a19db896c.description:
According to certain experts, the layout and architectural character of the Jesuit Church in Győr – besides the Italian patterns of Jesuit church architecture and the first church of the Order in Hungary in Nagyszombat (Trnava) – was influenced by the Jesuit Church in Vienna. Its layout (a nave with three adjoining closed chapels on both sides) later became an emblematic element in Hungarian Jesuit church architecture. On the side walls of the nave topped by a barrel vault, there is a tabernacle. The sanctuary has a rectangular end, and is the same width as the nave.  
Besides traditional Jesuit iconography, specific features of Hungarian iconography from the period can also be seen relating to the Ottoman wars and the closely related theme of the *Regnum Marianum/Patrona Hungariae* (St. Stephen offering the country to the Virgin Mary). All the saints, kings and bishops lined up on the decorative programme were founders and supporters of the Catholic Hungarian Kingdom, and defenders against the infidels or non-believers (images of Turks and Protestants appear on the altars).  
The Tyrolean painter, Paul Troger, painted the main altarpiece (*Apotheosis of St. Ignatius*) and also the ceiling mural in the sanctuary (*Ascension of St. Ignatius*) in 1744; the ceiling of the nave (*Annunciation*) in 1747 and the murals of the vault pendentives of four Prophets and four Evangelists (dated with Troger's signature beneath *St. Luke the Evangelist*) in 1744. The *trompe-l'œil* architectural wall painting and the ceiling of the sanctuary are by Gaetano Fanti.    
The main façade, completed by Martin (Athanasius) Wittwer a Carmelite architect around 1726, is articulated by statues in niches (St. John of Nepomuk, St. John the Evangelist, St. Andrew, St. Francis Borgia, the Virgin Mary and St. Ignatius of Loyola), by windows and volutes, two towers and the main stone gate (1641).  
Between 1743 and 1744, János Götzelmayer from Győr created the main altarpiece adorned by two columns and sculptures representing St. Peter, St. Joseph, St. John of Nepomuk and St. Paul (made by Josef Rössler \[Ressler\]) and the coat of arms of the patron, Prebendary Ádám Acsády.   
Acsády's coat of arms also appears on the triumphal arch. János Burghar(d)t from Győrsziget made the organ (1755–1757) and Mihály János Crines from Győr made the altar cross (c. 1710). The embossed pulpit was donated by Bishop Márton Padányi Bíró and made by Lajos Gode, a disciple of G. R. Donner, in 1748–1749.  József Ullydeszki made the *ciborium* in the mid-1780s. The furniture is by local craftsmen. Both the monastery refectory and the former Jesuit apothecary are decorated with stuccoes.
01a0ff11-5a79-51fe-9d67-b88a19db896c.short_description: The Jesuit Order settled in Győr in 1627 and played an important role in the Catholic spiritual renaissance (rooted in the Counter-Reformation movement) and the spread of Baroque art in Hungary. Building of the Jesuit Church dedicated to St. Ignatius of Loyola began in 1634/1635. The church was consecrated in 1641, but the interior decoration was not complete until the mid-18th century.
01a0ff11-5a79-51fe-9d67-b88a19db896c.method_for_datation: Based on written sources, signed artworks and stylistic research.

01a0ff11-5a79-51fe-9d67-b88a19db896c.history:
The Episcopate of Győr, founded by King Stephen I, flourished until the Turkish occupation of Hungary diminished its prosperity. Győr, where the bishop resided, was only under Turkish rule for a short period, but the army of Suleiman the Magnificent ravaged the Episcopate on its way to and from Vienna (1529; 1532). Following liberation from Turkish rule, the city, an important link in the chain of Hungarian strongholds, was unable to return to normalcy as its infrastructure was in a state of decay. During this period, the bishop resided in Győr for short periods only.  
Apart from nurturing and supporting the spiritual life of Catholics, the renaissance of Catholicism in the 17th century also fostered the reconstruction of the city's infrastructure. The Jesuit order settled in Győr in 1627 establishing the church (dedicated to the founder, St. Ignatius of Loyola), monastery and school. The Jesuits played a central role in the infrastructural restoration of Győr, as well as the spiritual, cultural and scientific life of the city, until the order was dissolved in 1733.  
The financial difficulties that beset the Jesuits meant that the construction and interior decoration of the church was largely financed by patrons, among which, Archbishop György Szelepcsényi, Prebendary Ádám Acsády, Bishop of Győr, other members of the chapter and the families of children that attended the Jesuit school.  
Scholars tend to attribute the plans of the church to an Italian master, Baccio del Bianco. The construction was supervised by the Italian Bartolomeo Torre (from 1634/1635 to 1641). After the church was consecrated in 1641, local benefactors helped to install the first altars in 1642. The second era of construction extended into the 18th century: the main altar, ceiling murals of the bay, the sanctuary, general interior decoration and decoration of the towers of the main façade. The nave took on its current form after reconstruction of the church in 1738.  
After the Jesuit order was dissolved in 1733, the Benedictines obtained the building complex in 1802. Today the church is a Roman Catholic parish church. In place of the former Jesuit school stands a Benedictine high school built in 1888. The former Jesuit pharmacy houses an Apothecary Museum.
01a0ff11-5a79-51fe-9d67-b88a19db896c.patrons: György Szelepcsényi, Archbishop of Esztergom (1595–1685); Ádám Acsády (1680–1744), Prebendary in Győr between 1713–1736 and Roman Catholic Bishop as of 1726; Márton Padányi Bíró (1696–1762) Bishop of Veszprém

05127f0b-387e-53fc-9c38-7c747e046530.name: Reliquary of St. Stephen the King
05127f0b-387e-53fc-9c38-7c747e046530.description:
The reliquary bust of St. Stephen the King, on a base, shows the saint in royal dress. Characteristics of the Baroque style come to the fore in the saint’s head shown in the round and almost imperceptibly turned sideways, with striking features and a soft wavy beard and moustache.  
The bust was probably made by a master craftsman from Rome, influenced by Bernini, while the crown is the work of a contemporary Central European goldsmith.  
The Latin inscription in a cartouche nailed to the front of the base records that Cardinal Francesco Barberini, nephew of Pope Urban VIII, had this bust made in 1635 out of piety for St. Stephen. He commissioned the bust to hold the saint’s skull, endowing the relic with the reverence it deserved. Today it is still in Zagreb Cathedral dedicated to St. Stephen the King.  
St. Stephen, King of Hungary, converted the Hungarians to Christianity and in the early 11th century founded an archbishopric in his hometown Esztergom where he died. He was canonised in 1087 and his cult spread from Hungary to Croatia where it was especially widespread after the Middle Ages. At the time, Hungary and Croatia were in a union and known as the lands of the Crown of St. Stephen after the crown he wore.
05127f0b-387e-53fc-9c38-7c747e046530.short_description: The reliquary of St. Stephen in the form of a bust shows him dressed as a king with a crown on his head. The bust was probably the work of a master craftsman from Rome, influenced by Bernini, while the crown is attributed to a goldsmith from the Central European circle. The Latin inscription in a cartouche on the front of the base verifies that the reliquary was commissioned by Cardinal Barberini in 1635, nephew of Pope Urban VIII, a member of a powerful and wealthy Roman family that died out in the male line in 1736.
05127f0b-387e-53fc-9c38-7c747e046530.method_for_datation:
The 1915 Inventory of Zagreb Cathedral mentions the reliquary.  
A Latin inscription with the year of origin is on a cartouche on the front of the base.
05127f0b-387e-53fc-9c38-7c747e046530.obtention: Cardinal Francesco Barberini gifted the reliquary to Zagreb Cathedral.

11cedc74-b01f-5257-950e-dec5d9f42b78.name: Baroque Bridge
11cedc74-b01f-5257-950e-dec5d9f42b78.description: The stone bridge is 74.8 m long, 8 m wide and 6.2 m high. It connects the chateau and the area below it with the former feudal town. The investors explained the presence of the limestone statues on the bridge by saying that “even strangers passing by could worship God in public through His saints, to the disgrace of heretics”. The bridge is located on a major communication route connecting Brno and Třebíč, Telč and Jindřichův Hradec. The selection of saints was made with respect to the personal piousness of the investors and their families.
11cedc74-b01f-5257-950e-dec5d9f42b78.short_description: The stone bridge connects the chateau and the area below it with the former feudal town. It is lined with statues of saints, the objective being that “even strangers passing by may worship God in public through His saints, to the disgrace of heretics”. The bridge is located on a major communication route between Brno and Třebíč, Telč and Jindřichův Hradec. Preparatory sketches for some of the statues have survived. The selection of saints was made with respect to the personal piousness of the investors and their families. Similar bridges are found chiefly in Bohemia where they were modelled on Charles Bridge in Prague and enhanced by statues of c. 1720. The overall prototype was Ponte d´Angeli, Rome.
11cedc74-b01f-5257-950e-dec5d9f42b78.method_for_datation: The bridge features commemorative plaques, and the construction costs are recorded in the demesne accounts.

11cedc74-b01f-5257-950e-dec5d9f42b78.history: The bridge was built by the owner of the demesne on the site of a former bridge across the Oslava that was torn down by a flood. His descendants had it set with a series of 20 statues. The designs and eight of the statues are by J. Winterhalder Sr., the remainder are by A. Jelínek. Winterhalder created over 30 statues and further decorations for the demesne. In 1752 the demesne was purchased by the Haugwitzs who presided over it until 1945. Similar bridges are found chiefly in Bohemia, where they were modelled on Charles Bridge in Prague and enhanced by statues of c. 1720. The overall prototype was Ponte d´Angeli, Rome.

14d23909-007c-5bfe-ba51-0f21c11eaef4.name: Namban Oratory
14d23909-007c-5bfe-ba51-0f21c11eaef4.description:
This rectangular oratory surmounted by a triangular pediment with the monogram *IHS* (the abbreviation of the Greek *IHSOUS*, or JESUS) located at the centre, has two side-panels enclosing a painting of the Virgin Mary holding the infant Jesus. Although the lacquer decoration presents a predominantly Japanese ornamental grammar – especially a floral one – both its form and the iconography embody Christian cultural references. The pictorial image is itself an example of the possible interaction between the Jesuit painting school – operating in Japan since the 1580s – and the Japanese pupils that quickly demonstrated skill in Western-style painting.  
As it is, such a hybrid object, that crosses different artistic backgrounds, could only have been made during the Portuguese presence in Japan, during the period spanning approximately 1549 to 1640.  
The oratory is mentioned in the *Inventário Artístico de Santarém* (Santarém Artistic Inventory) as Indo-Portuguese lacquer work. Such misinformation reveals how, in the middle of the 20th century, such an item was unfamiliar to the European public in general, but that was not the case in the late 16th and beginning of the 17th century, at least not for the Portuguese elite. Such a statement can only be based on the remaining objects – with or without associated painting – the number of which has expanded increasingly during the last three decades (this example did not come to light until 1985). A fact that also draws attention to the demands of the Iberian market for these objects at the time.  
The Sardoal Oratory has the particularity of being associated with a religious space, thanks to an inscription located on the altar of Nossa Senhora da Esperança in the Church of Nossa Senhora da Caridade. This text, dated 1670, is the earliest known reference in Portugal to a reminiscent *Namban* object.
14d23909-007c-5bfe-ba51-0f21c11eaef4.short_description: A lacquered *Namban* oratory with a floral design in gold and silver powder (*maki-e)* and mother of pearl inlay (*raden*) with a painting of the Virgin Mary holding the infant Jesus.

14d23909-007c-5bfe-ba51-0f21c11eaef4.method_for_datation: The date and origin of the object were established on stylistic grounds and partially by the inscription (see text above).
14d23909-007c-5bfe-ba51-0f21c11eaef4.obtention: The object was transferred from the church of Nossa Senhora da Caridade to the Santa Casa da Misericórdia.

16dcfff2-c980-5426-8a0a-5dd422372da2.name: Catholic Plague Chapel of Ss. Sebastian, Roch and Pirmin
16dcfff2-c980-5426-8a0a-5dd422372da2.alternate_name: “Burschlkirche” or “Pestheiligenkirche” (Church of Plague Saints / Church on the Hill)
16dcfff2-c980-5426-8a0a-5dd422372da2.description: The Burschlkirche is an important example of the survival of older stylistic forms within Early Baroque. The choir with its stuccoed net vault is entirely executed in the Late Gothic style. In contrast, the magnificent panelled ceiling of the flat-roofed nave is a reminiscence of the Renaissance, echoing the festive halls in castles and palaces. However, the carved altars which lend the church its national importance, are typical works of the Early Baroque with monumental column aedicules, although a number of the individual forms display Late Gothic and Mannerist influences.
16dcfff2-c980-5426-8a0a-5dd422372da2.short_description: The small votive church received its name from the location on which it is built: the “Burschl”, a hill belonging to the district of Perfuch, on whose flank it is picturesquely situated overlooking the town. Its importance is due to the interior work, above all the exquisite mid-17th-century Early Baroque carved altars, the work of local master craftsmen, and the nave’s panelled ceiling.
16dcfff2-c980-5426-8a0a-5dd422372da2.method_for_datation: Documentation of consecration, altars with inscriptions naming donors, archives
16dcfff2-c980-5426-8a0a-5dd422372da2.bibliography: *Barock in Landeck.* *Kunstwerke aus der Burschlkirche und der Pfarrkirche zu Unserer Lieben Frau*. Innsbruck 1990.
16dcfff2-c980-5426-8a0a-5dd422372da2.history: The building, on which work began in 1650, has its origins in a vow made by the Weinzierl family during the plague of 1635/36. The consecration held in 1656 is documented. The building was altered in the spirit of historicism during the restoration of 1899 and again in 1936. During a further period of restoration between 1980 and 1990 it was restored to its original appearance.
16dcfff2-c980-5426-8a0a-5dd422372da2.architects: Altar figures attributed to the sculptors: Adam Payr (?–1682), Michael Lechleitner (1614–1669); altarpiece attributed to: Michael Waldmann the younger (1640–1682)
keywords: Votive church; Early Baroque; carved altars; panelled ceiling

178f74aa-fe42-524b-94f2-f5d4a1c1bd50.name: Processional Altar of St. John the Evangelist
178f74aa-fe42-524b-94f2-f5d4a1c1bd50.description:
A silver processional altar made at the beginning of the 18th century, which belonged to the Royal Monastery of Our Lady of Conception, and was used in the Procession of the Holy Sacrament in Beja. The social and religious significance of the Corpus Christi Day procession cannot be understated; it represents one of the greatest manifestations of the Portuguese Baroque, which once acknowledged, justifies the sumptuousness of some of the pieces used in these ceremonies. Traditionally, up until 1893, the altar was carried by farmers.  
Rectangular in shape, the *acroteria* (small bases placed at the four extremities) has a beaded edging, and four *albarradas* or ornamental vases, alternate with smaller jars in the middle. The entirety is covered with vegetable and scalloped-shell ornamentation, and St. James' crosses. The wooden carrying rods are also silver plated.  
The octagonal shaped pedestal stands over the main body, decorated with double scalloped-shell ornamentation, pear-shaped “tables” and St. James' crosses. There is also an octagonal platform with small jars placed at each corner of the pedestal.  
An iron column rises above the pedestal, covered with silk cloth embroidered with gold thread. It meets a gold and silver halo embellished with precious stones above which a gold and silver crown rests, also studded with precious stones. In the middle of the altarpiece, the Martyrdom of St. John the Evangelist is played out, the saint graphically shown immersed in boiling olive oil. The wooden effigy of the saint with clasped hands looks straight up at the sky. The silver boiler, standing on a silver tripod above the fire, is kept alight by two multicoloured wooden figures, kneeling at either side of the boiler. One of them is blowing and the other is using a solid-silver pitchfork.  
The patrons of the altarpiece were a group of nuns devoted to St. John the Evangelist. There was another group of nuns in the same convent that devoted themselves to St. John the Baptist and commissioned a similar processional altar in honour of the saint. In fact, both altarpieces date from the beginning of the 18th century and were made in the same workshop. They both show the same crowned stamps of the city of Lisbon and the same maker's letter “M”.
178f74aa-fe42-524b-94f2-f5d4a1c1bd50.short_description: A silver processional altar made at the beginning of the 18th century, it portrays features typical of the Portuguese Baroque at the time of King João V. Designed to represent the Martyrdom of St. John the Evangelist, the piece belonged to the Royal Monastery of Our Lady of Conception and was used in the procession of the Holy Sacrament in Beja, on Corpus Christi Day.

17f9a63f-8638-5603-ac11-f8d674b5657b.name: *Firework Display Held in Brno on the Occasion of the Coronation of a Picture of the Virgin Mary of St. Thomas*
17f9a63f-8638-5603-ac11-f8d674b5657b.description:
In the 1730s Moravia hosted two festive events offsetting the largest religious festivals of the Czech baroque, the beatification and canonisation of St. John of Nepomuk in Prague (1729). As the capital of the Czech kingdom came into the spotlight for the whole country, so the celebrations of the coronation of Marian pictures symbolically confirmed the importance of Olomouc and Brno, the two main towns in the Moravian margraviate. These occasions made the Holy Virgin the Queen of Moravia and the patron saint of the country. The festivities around the coronation of the picture of the Virgin Mary in Brno lasted a week. “The night turned into day and the town of Brno into a new heavenly Jerusalem full of scenes of adoration, praise and exultation”. The town's splendour was illuminated by 5,000 lights and plentiful firework displays. The print shows one of the ephemeral festive structures with sculpted decoration and pyrotechnical effects. A detailed programme was issued to accompany the fireworks, explaining the display to viewers in 27 steps.  
After a fanfare of trumpets and tympani, the fireworks were set off by the firing of cannons, and an angel setting white and red fire to the chronogram “Mary the Gem and Patron Saint of the Town of Brno”. Rockets lit up six life-size figures: Emperor Charles IV, who donated the picture, his brother Jan Jindřich, founder of the Augustinian monastery, Pope Clement XII, protector of the adoration picture, the Bishop of Olomouc, who crowned the picture, the prior of the monastery, and the *genius loci* of Brno. The spectacle climaxed with Catherine Wheels at the tips of pyramids and six hearts burning under the figures. The fountain in the foreground started to spew a multitude of tiny stars and blue flowers, while the fire illuminated a flood of garlands. The final highlight of the show, to an overture of cannon fire, was the flight of a two-headed imperial eagle rising with an inscription within mighty flames.
17f9a63f-8638-5603-ac11-f8d674b5657b.short_description: Celebrations for the coronation of Marian pictures symbolically confirmed the importance of Olomouc and Brno, the two main towns of the Moravian margraviate. The Holy Virgin became Queen and patron saint of Moravia. The print shows one of the ephemeral festive structures with pyrotechnical effects.
17f9a63f-8638-5603-ac11-f8d674b5657b.method_for_datation: Marked bottom left: *F. A. Baran del;* bottom right: *F. A. Mayer Sculp: Brunae*. The little-known F. A. Baran was the artist and engraver of the fireworks print. František Antonín Mayer, a student of Jan Jiří Guttwein, was a bookbinder and engraver in Brno. He executed the engraving of the “silver altar” and the picture of the Brno Thaumaturga.
17f9a63f-8638-5603-ac11-f8d674b5657b.obtention: Purchased in 1978 from an art shop in Brno.

183f3b05-4be1-5afa-b61c-38f98717b91a.name: *Adoration of the Painting of the Virgin Mary of Znojmo*
183f3b05-4be1-5afa-b61c-38f98717b91a.description:
The image within, praised by angels, is a painted reproduction of an adoration picture of the Virgin Mary of Znojmo which originated in the 1630s. Its subject is the miraculous transportation of the picture which, according to legend, was brought to its new location by angels. The gloomy landscape in the bottom section of the painting has, beyond doubt, an allegorical meaning, while the illuminated adoration image presents a reality higher than the earthly life, here represented by thistles, military fortresses and rocks. The artist accentuated the difference between the miraculous picture and mundane reality through quaint, rustic elements in the picture of the Virgin Mary, in terms appropriate to chronology and the taste of the period. On the other hand, the figures of the angels and the landscape are rendered in Herdt’s trademark warm red-brown and golden tones, revealing his Flemish training.  
This sizeable painting is an example of the then popular picture-within-a-picture type. The intention of such paintings was to visually enhance, or “update”, well-known and already worshipped miracle-inspiring pictures. These “miraculous” pictures were displayed on altars, like relics, and as such were to be venerated. At the same time, pictures-within-pictures were employed, by Counter-Reformation and missionary orders in particular, for more striking presentations of “miraculous” pictures among ordinary town and country people.  
The origination of the painting marks a key moment in the history of the worship of the miraculous Znojmo picture, since the burgeoning importance of the Znojmo Dominicans in South Moravia involved the cult of the Virgin Mary of Znojmo. One of the first mentions of a Marian brotherhood of the Holy Rosary, active in one of the chapels of the monastery complex, date to the same period. In 1734 the “miraculous picture” was festively crowned and placed on a new altar in the monastery church.
183f3b05-4be1-5afa-b61c-38f98717b91a.short_description: The canvas is typical of the picture-within-a-picture approach of the time, intended to visually “update” miracle-inspiring pictures. Rustic elements used in the painting within the painting contrast the sacred with the mundane; the warmly rendered angels and landscape reveal the artist’s Flemish training.
183f3b05-4be1-5afa-b61c-38f98717b91a.method_for_datation: The painting is signed and dated 1678. The Dominican monastery, established in Znojmo around the mid-13th century, suffered serious damage during the Thirty Years' War and was not substantially restored until several decades later. At that time, *The Invention of the Holy Cross*, a painting by Jan Daniel (de) Herdt a Dutch artist formerly active in Brescia, Italy, was obtained for the main altar. A year later, Herdt painted another canvas for the monastery, its subject being the adoration of a picture of the Virgin Mary of Znojmo.
183f3b05-4be1-5afa-b61c-38f98717b91a.obtention: The painting was probably found in one of the chapels of the Dominican monastery church in Znojmo which was pulled down in the late 19th century. The picture was transferred to Znojmo Castle chapel, administered by the Museum of Znojmo since the early 20th century.

20d226c3-47f8-5bd5-ab51-56f759018dff.name: Zelená Hora, Church of St. John of Nepomuk
20d226c3-47f8-5bd5-ab51-56f759018dff.description: The church construction combines two chief motifs, a tongue, and a five-pointed star, creating a unique building. The expansive intertwining shapes and movement of light provide it with a striking dynamism. Here, V. Vejmluva established a “spiritual mausoleum” for John of Nepomuk, a saint canonised in 1729, and whose cult became one of the most widespread in Central Europe.
20d226c3-47f8-5bd5-ab51-56f759018dff.short_description: This pilgrimage church is one of the most remarkable buildings in Czech lands. It combines two main motifs: a tongue, and a five-pointed star. The expansive, intertwining shapes and movement of light provide the geometrical central building with a striking dynamism. The building mythologizes in visual form a previously insignificant place and presents its origin as a divine miracle. It was here that a learned abbot of the Cistercian Monastery established a “spiritual mausoleum” for John of Nepomuk, a saint canonised in 1729, and whose cult became one of the most widespread in Central Europe.

20d226c3-47f8-5bd5-ab51-56f759018dff.history: The establishment of the church was associated with the upcoming beatification and canonisation of John of Nepomuk after his miraculously intact tongue had been found in his grave in St. Vitus Cathedral, Prague. The construction was initiated by V. Vejmluva, abbot of the nearby Cistercian Monastery, who named the hill above it after Zelená Hora, near Nepomuk, the martyr’s birthplace and the place from which the first Cistercians came to Žďár. In 1722 the church was consecrated and construction work continued with cloisters with five chapels and five gates. After the architect’s death, the complex was completed by F. B. Klíčník who was, like Santini, a member of the Penitent Brotherhood in the monastery which was founded in 1722.

2b8bffd7-5ba3-5029-b6c5-d671a0482187.name: High altar for San Pietro Cathedral of Bologna
2b8bffd7-5ba3-5029-b6c5-d671a0482187.description:
This complex and precious altar was donated by Pope Lambertini to the San Pietro Cathedral of Bologna. Originally it was composed of six candlesticks, a silver cross and a silver frontal depicting *Jesus Handing the Keys to St. Peter in the Presence of the Apostles*. Unfortunately, these rich objects were probably handed to the Frenchmen in 1796, after the treaty of Tolentino, signed by Pope Pius VII.  
The invoices for the high altar are registered in the *Diario Benedettino*. The pope prayed that it reached Bologna safe and sound.  
In the middle of the side there is a silver embossed oval representing *Christ Rescuing Peter from the Water*, on the sides are two smaller roundels representing allegories of *Faith*. The three bas-reliefs are framed in gilded cast bronze, with cherubs' heads and garlands against a blue lapis-lazuli background. In the corners the oval bas-reliefs represent the *Martyrdom of St. Peter* on the left and *St. Peter in Jail Visited by the Angel*. On the upper side hangs the coat of arms of the Lambertini family in silver.  
The whole altar is on show together with a sumptuous frontal donated by the pope in 1742, made of  
hemp canvas embroidered with gold thread. Against the embroidered gold background are several sewn gold leaf decorations. In the middle is a roundel of *St. Peter* half bust and on the sides the coat of arms of the Lambertinis' with the tiara and the papal keys held by angels.  
This extremely precious altar, only a part of the richer original complex, is characterised by its technical skill and high artistic quality. The Roman silversmith Angelo Spinazzi, documented from 1721 to 1767, probably made the step. On the sides a hallmark, despite being not entirely legible is believed to be that of the Roman craftsman Filippo Tofani. No hallmark is visible on the main central relief.
2b8bffd7-5ba3-5029-b6c5-d671a0482187.short_description:
This extremely precious altar was donated to the cathedral of Bologna by Pope Benedict XIV.  
The sides and corners are characterised by extremely detailed work: against a blue lapis-lazuli ground are intertwined coats of arms of the Lambertini family and oval bas-reliefs with figures in chiselled and embossed silver and gilded bronze. On the side, in the middle, *Christ Rescues Peter from the Water* flanked by two Allegories of Faith, on the corners *St. Peter in Prison Visited by the Angel* and the *Martyrdom of St. Peter*. The work was made in Roman workshops. The altar is completed by a beautifully worked frontal, also a gift from Pope Benedict XIV (1742).
2b8bffd7-5ba3-5029-b6c5-d671a0482187.dimensions: Side max. 57x380x27 cm; medallions left and right 34x25 cm, central 35x55 cm; sides 105x78 cm, 5x63 cm; capitals height 57 cm; roundels, right 30x21 cm, left 28x21 cm; frontal 104,5x355 cm
2b8bffd7-5ba3-5029-b6c5-d671a0482187.method_for_datation:
This altar was sent to Bologna and began in 1753. Work continued to 1756 although the whole complex was not yet complete.  
Spinacci, quoted many times as the author of the step, might be Angelo Spinazzi, a Roman silversmith working between 1721 and 1767.  
On the reliefs on the corners it is possible to see two hallmarks: 1) *the cipher 85 in a circle*, 2) *FT with a small cross under inside an irregular frame*. The first is used by several testers and affirms the high quality silver, following 1734 prescriptions. The second hallmark refers to the silversmith Tofani, even if this work is not cited by Bulgari in his monograph and if we don't know for sure the hallmark of this master.

2f04166a-1867-5f2a-bc57-934a78292a79.name: Tomb of Bishop D. Manuel de Moura Manuel
2f04166a-1867-5f2a-bc57-934a78292a79.description:
The Tomb of Bishop D. Manuel de Moura Manuel is based on a traditional French model seen in, for example, the Tomb of Cardinal Richelieu at the Sorbonne in Paris. Laprade introduced a new typology to Portugal: a tomb with an architectural background filled with allegorical figures. The inclusion of funerary symbolism and its association with the allegories of Life and Death are adjusted to fit in with the Baroque spirit. At a time when abstract and formal caskets in cases were the norm this was an innovation in Portugal. The tomb was created in the artist's studio in Coimbra.  
In terms of the architectural composition, the pilasters are transformed into Atlantes representing crying women who stage the sorrow of death with veils that partially hide their faces. The mournful tone of these figures contrast with the graceful angels that flit about in an oval-shaped plaque carrying with them the coat of arms of D. Manuel. At the top and bottom of the beam, are *putti* seen together with symbols of Life and Death. The tympanum is decorated with the figure of Time – an allegory of Death – accompanied by an angel that holds the bishop's crosier. The close of the tombstone arch is furnished with a Phoenix – symbol of the Resurrection and celestial Life. The sense of movement is remarkable in the flowing sideways of Time's clothes and the curvature of the prostrate body of D. Manuel. The naturalist portrait of D. Manuel, with one hand on his chest gazing at the image of Our Lady, suggests that he is waiting for the final verdict. Watching over the scene is the macabre skeletal figure of a magistrate wearing a bay-leaf crown – symbolic of the transition from life to death – wearing an amulet with a *Memento Mori* distich.
2f04166a-1867-5f2a-bc57-934a78292a79.short_description: A limestone tomb showing the deceased, Bishop D. Manuel de Moura Manuel, prostrate accompanied by the allegorical figures of Justice, Fortitude, Faith, Charity and Time, and the religious scene of the Appearance of Our Lady of Penha de França in bas-relief.

31e3813f-0fcd-5e04-9091-f647c9b7e674.name: Pilgrimage Church of the Elevation of the Holy Cross, Jaroměřice u Jevíčka
31e3813f-0fcd-5e04-9091-f647c9b7e674.description: Stations of the Cross with obelisks featuring reliefs of the Suffering Christ start in Jaroměřice at the Church of All Hallows. The pilgrimage area, enclosed by a high wall with semi-circular bastions (chapels), is entered through a gate known as the House of Pilate, with two towers and a sculpture of *Ecce Homo*. Arcades within the cloister contain remnants of frescos with scenes from the Torture of Christ. Near the fenced area is a building on a ground plan of St. Andrew's cross: two arms (in the Jaroměřice direction) make up a parsonage, the other two contain a Loreto Chapel with tombs of the Augustinians who administered the complex. The interior features period semi-folk furnishing.
31e3813f-0fcd-5e04-9091-f647c9b7e674.short_description: This extraordinary pilgrimage complex was to mediate Christ’s suffering and death. The site location evokes Golgotha, with the church as a metaphorical representation of the temple of Jerusalem. The architecture demonstrates that J. J. Santini-Aichel’s spectacular designs were not unique to his time, and that his concepts found response even outside major art centres. Striking, semi-folk interiors enhance the mystical air. The pilgrimage tradition was strong in the country; there were about 140 sites where pilgrims gathered in order to “find the wellspring of all virtue”.
31e3813f-0fcd-5e04-9091-f647c9b7e674.method_for_datation: The founder of the present “Calvary” was F. M. Šubíř (1680–1738), who decided to expand the chapel to express his gratitude for the preservation of his wife’s life in childbirth.
31e3813f-0fcd-5e04-9091-f647c9b7e674.bibliography:
Emanuel Poche (ed), *Umělecké památky Čech 1, A-J*, Prague, 1978, pp. 573–575.

Dirk De Meyer, Johann Santini Aichl, *Architectuur et ambiguiteit* I-II, Eindhoven, 1997, p. 547.  
Mojmír Horyna, *Jan Blažej Santini-Aichl*, Prague, 1998, pp. 413–415, nos. 31, 32.
31e3813f-0fcd-5e04-9091-f647c9b7e674.history: South of Jaroměřice towers a steep hill associated with a legend of the evil spirit Kudrman. In 1664 a cross was erected on it and masses took place there. In around 1680 as thanks for averting a plague epidemic, a chapel was built on the hill, dedicated to St. Fabian, St. Sebastian, St. Roch and St. Rosalia, protectors from the plague. The founder of the present “Calvary” was F. M. Šubíř, who decided to expand the chapel to express his gratitude for the preservation of his wife’s life in childbirth. On the recommendation of a pilgrim from the Holy Land, to whom the Jaromerice hill bore some resemblance to Jerusalem’s Golgotha, the Church of the Elevation of the Holy Cross was constructed. Further buildings with Biblical connotations to Christ’s martyrdom were subsequently added. In 1735 the Arch-brotherhood of the Holy Saviour was established there. Similar associations also operated in Rome and Krakow. The pilgrimage tradition was strong in the country; there were about 140 sites where pilgrims gathered in order to “find the wellspring of all virtue”.

32629ea7-5978-5c34-ac5e-6fa3012db355.name: Reliquary Chest of St. João de Brito
32629ea7-5978-5c34-ac5e-6fa3012db355.description:
The Portuguese established trading posts along the coasts of India and China where merchants could trade and store their merchandise, extending their authority into the hinterland. While the traditional political structures of local chieftains remained, the elite profited by reselling European wares. In addition to trade, the Portuguese sought to spread Christianity among the local Asian populations with Franciscan, Dominican and later Jesuit missionaries preaching to the indigenous peoples. The Christian missionaries learned the native languages, familiarised themselves with the indigenous cultures and even their religions; in this effort, the Jesuits were extremely dedicated. St. João de Brito was sent as a member of the Jesuit Order to the mission of Maduré, in India, in 1673. His aim was to convert the higher castes, in order to better establish Christianity in the region. He became a *pandaraswami*, an Indian ascetic. One of his converts, Prince Tadaya Theva upon becoming Christian, was rejected by one of his wives. She complained to her uncle, the Raja of Marava, who had the Jesuit executed in Orbyur, India, in 1690.  
This chest, with a pyramidal lid engraved in low-relief, features scenes of St. João de Brito's life and martyrdom. The bas-relief on the top features the saint in Indian dress, with sandals and a staff. Several winged cherubs in chiselled silver flank the lid. The body of the chest presents two sculpted winged angels on each side in true Baroque expression. Four elaborate feet in gilded silver hold the main body. Commissioned by King Pedro II of Portugal as a royal homage to the Jesuit saint, the Portuguese coat of arms is seen in the centre testifying to the royal provenance.  
The presence of the *Agnus Dei* on the top may have been a later addition by the Jesuits, who used it on special occasions as a Eucharistic tabernacle for the veneration of the Blessed Sacrament.
32629ea7-5978-5c34-ac5e-6fa3012db355.short_description: Commissioned by King D. Pedro II, this Reliquary Chest is engraved in low-relief with scenes of St. João de Brito’s life and martyrdom. The bas-relief on the top features the saint in Indian dress, with sandals and a staff.

3b78fd39-550c-5644-9e94-61b43dc61c5f.name: Vranov nad Dyjí Chateau
3b78fd39-550c-5644-9e94-61b43dc61c5f.description: The chateau towers over the valley from a rocky promontory above the River Dyje in the Podyjí National Park. Of the original castle two prismatic towers, part of the ramparts and buildings in the outer bailey, have been preserved. Its well-devised fortification system became part of the reconstruction concept to glorify an ancient dynasty by means of a “*via triumphalis*”, the principal feature of which is the unique Hall of the Ancestors perched upon the promontory.
3b78fd39-550c-5644-9e94-61b43dc61c5f.short_description: This spectacular chateau above a meander of the River Dyje is one of the most remarkable buildings of mid-European Baroque. A well-devised fortification system became part of the reconstruction concept to glorify an ancient dynasty by means of “*via triumphalis*”, the principal feature of which is the unique Hall of the Ancestors perched on a rocky promontory. The design of the chateau is typical of the Habsburg Empire style. The decoration is the work of major Viennese artists with Italian leanings.
3b78fd39-550c-5644-9e94-61b43dc61c5f.method_for_datation: The fresco in the Hall of the Ancestors is signed and dated; further information follows from correspondence and archive documents.

3b78fd39-550c-5644-9e94-61b43dc61c5f.history: The chateau came into existence through the reconstruction of an old Romanesque-Gothic castle situated above a meander of the River Dyje. After a fire in 1665, Michael Jan II of Althann erected the impressive Hall of the Ancestors and a chapel to the design of imperial architect, Fischer von Erlach. Under Countess Marie Felicita and Michael Josef the chateau interiors were rebuilt in the classicist style. The provincial barrister, J. Hilgartner of Lilienborn, who acquired the demesne through bankruptcy proceedings, took up the original concept and put much effort into the completion of a landscaped park, which bears traces of pre-Romanticism and a Rousseauesque relationship with nature. Major building changes occurred in the 19th century when the demesne was owned by the Mniszeks, an aristocratic family from Poland. In 1938 Vranov became part of Hitler’s Third Reich; the chateau was confiscated and sold to Baron Gebhard von der Wense-Mörse. It has been state property since 1945.

3cae71c8-dbf2-536f-bbdd-73e3c7e29ff5.name: *Crucifixion*
3cae71c8-dbf2-536f-bbdd-73e3c7e29ff5.description:
The Dominican Monastery of St. Domingos de Benfica, founded in 1399 on the outskirts of Lisbon, was rebuilt in the second quarter of the 17th century during the government of Friar João de Vasconcelos (1624–1632). During this period Manuel Pereira was commissioned to make a series of sculptural devotional images among which were the *Crucifixion* and *Our Lady of the Rosary* – both located over the aisle altars – and *Saint Dominique of Gusmão* and *St. Peter the Martyr* in the main arch niches.  
Portuguese Manuel Pereira studied in Rome and lived in Spain where he received important commissions from the Madrid court, which at the time was the capital of the Iberian monarchy (1580–1640). Pereira worked in stone, wood and alabaster, and using these materials he conceived mainly devotional sculptures that visually imparted the values inherited from the Trent Council through the dual rhetoric of *docere* and *delectare* (to teach, to move and to delight), aimed at heightening the inner conversion of the Christian. Manuel Pereira's sculptures are characterised by their dynamic composition, combined with the delicate treatment of the surfaces, which in their smallest details irradiate light, delivering a deep and intense psychology. These aesthetic values are present in the polychrome wooden sculptures of the *Immaculate Conception* in Toledo, *St. Ignatius of Loyola*, *St. Francis Xavier*, *St. Aloysus Gonzaga* and *St. Francis of Borja* commissioned by the Church of São Roque in Lisbon. One can include the *Crucifixions* in Cartuja de Miraflores in Burgos and St. Domingos de Benfica in Lisbon, where the realism and inner drama are remarkably intense. In the São Roque Benfica *Crucifixion,* based on an engraving by Pontius from a painting by Peter Paul Rubens, Pereira's Christ hangs lifeless and heavy from the cross, His face contorted, exhaling His last breath and His eyes closing slowly in agony.
3cae71c8-dbf2-536f-bbdd-73e3c7e29ff5.short_description: The epitome of Manuel Pereira's sculpture lies in his Crucifixions among which this one, in the Church of St. Domingos de Benfica, is remarkably intense. Based on a composition by Rubens, Christ's heavy, lifeless body hangs from the cross, creating a deep and intense psychological tension that visually imparts the values inherited from the Trent Council through the dual rhetoric of *docere* and *delectare* (to teach, to move and to delight), which in this context suggests that the body is elevated to eternity through the inner drama of the Passion.

3f0aa8ee-e226-51cc-bcf3-336f58df8d28.name: Church of Nossa Senhora dos Prazeres
3f0aa8ee-e226-51cc-bcf3-336f58df8d28.description:
The church of Beja (1672) has a quadrangular nave covered by a tunnel vault; a narrower and lower chancel, a semi-circular apse – finished with a cupola and louvre – and a quadrangular addorsed sacristy, also covered with a vault.  
The church is an excellent example of a “total work of art” or *gesamtkunstwerk*, a sensibility often associated with Baroque interiors. The interior, a *theatrum* *sacrum*, holds within it the wood carvings of Manuel João da Fonseca and Francisco da Silva, which reflect the dialogue between the artistic schools of Lisbon and Évora. The ceiling compositions by Pedro Figueira, António de Oliveira Bernardes and João Pereira Pegado, who were influenced by the Beja masters, continue the artistic dialogue. Oliveira Bernardes' canvases and Gabriel del Barco's tile work represent the Mysteries of the Life of the Virgin, enhancing the theme of the Immaculate Conception.
3f0aa8ee-e226-51cc-bcf3-336f58df8d28.short_description: The church of Nossa Senhora dos Prazeres in Beja lies close to the medieval city wall. Built in veneration of Our Lady, its importance was intensified by a miracle said to have taken place on a farm in Lisbon in the 16th century. Later, during the reign of King Pedro II, the church underwent renovation, turning it into one of the best examples of “plain” architecture and interior decoration in the Lower Alentejo. A remarkable example of a “Golden Church”, it is enriched with *azulejos*, gilded woodcarving, wall painting and canvases devoted to the Mysteries of the Life of Virgin, focusing on the co-existence of the Seven Sorrows and the Seven Joys of the Mother of God.
3f0aa8ee-e226-51cc-bcf3-336f58df8d28.bibliography: Serrão, V., Lameira, F., Falcão, J. A., *A Igreja de Nossa Senhora dos Prazeres em Beja, Arte e História de um Espaço Barroco (1672–1698),* Lisbon, 2007.
3f0aa8ee-e226-51cc-bcf3-336f58df8d28.history: During the 16th century a door was opened in the medieval wall of Beja allowing access to the main square, near the *Corredoura* (a road used for horse racing). Our Lady of Pleasures Church was built in veneration of the Miracle of Our Lady and to eulogise the Seven Sorrows and the Seven Joys of the Mother of God, the importance of which was further intensified by a miracle said to have taken place on a farm near Lisbon. According to tradition, the Virgin appeared to a girl and asked her to tell her parents and neighbours that a chapel should be built close by. Thereafter, a series of other miracles aroused intense devotional outbreaks in the country and overseas territories, and these accelerated the construction of even more places of worship.

40184ca3-ec39-5539-8d0e-9cdab4ab323e.name: National Palace of Mafra
40184ca3-ec39-5539-8d0e-9cdab4ab323e.description:
Symmetrically organised, the building evolves from a central axis: the basilica flanked by the palace façades, the king's apartments at the north end, and the queen's on the south. At the back there is a convent, originally intended for the Order of St. Francis, which has at its nucleus a uniquely well-preserved 18th-century hospital.  
Altogether the palace occupies 38,000 m2 and has 1,200 rooms and 4,700 doors and windows. The high points of the Basilica are the ensemble of statues made by Italian masters, part of The Royal Commission that also comprises an important collection of 18th-century Italian and Portuguese paintings, two Flemish-made carillons with 92 bells, retables from the Mafra school of sculpture, and a set of six organs.
40184ca3-ec39-5539-8d0e-9cdab4ab323e.short_description: The National Palace of Mafra is Portugal’s most important Baroque building, comprising a royal palace, a basilica and a Franciscan convent within which is a well-preserved 18th-century hospital. The palace houses the remarkable Royal Commission, a collection of Italian sculptures and Portuguese and Italian paintings, two carillons and six historical organs as well as precious gold artefacts and church ornaments.

40184ca3-ec39-5539-8d0e-9cdab4ab323e.history:
Taking advantage of the prosperity granted by the Brazilian gold afflux, King D. João V ordered construction of the Palace in the hope that this initiative would bless him with the birth of a male heir to the throne. The first stone was set in 1717, under the direction of the architect Johan Frederich Ludwig.  
The so-called “Real Obra” was the first Portuguese school of Fine Arts, particularly for architects, stonemasons, carpenters, cabinetmakers and painters; in 1753, King D. João V’s son, King D. José I, implemented a School of Sculpture there under the direction of the Italian Alessandro Giusti.  
Mafra was King D. João V’s favourite palace, and at the end of the 18th century, he commissioned the mural paintings and a new ensemble of six organs for the Basilica. Although the palace was never a permanent royal residence, it was frequently visited by royalty for hunting in the extensive park or to attend religious festivities.  
In the aftermath of the monarchy’s last days, it was from Mafra that the last Portuguese sovereign, D. Manuel II, left to go into exile in 1910.

44cf7449-7064-5e7b-8625-27f3fafdff19.name: Processional cross
44cf7449-7064-5e7b-8625-27f3fafdff19.alternate_name: Processional standard of the brotherhood of the Tears of the Virgin Mary or of the Ponte del Borgo, later del Borgo, later Company of the Holy Sacrament
44cf7449-7064-5e7b-8625-27f3fafdff19.description:
This solemn gilded cross bears a rich decoration of vine leaves and vine-shoots made with a drill. There are interspersed with cherub heads and angels carved in the round, crowned with polychrome flowers and holding the instruments of the Passion of Christ.  
The branches resemble tree trunks with bark and knots. They end with two small knobs. The dead Christ in the middle is carved in the round, polychrome with an ample gilded cloth around his hips. On the upper part of the longitudinal arm hangs a cartouche with the writing \`INRI\` held by three small angels.  
Along the lower sides, stand on shelves four small statues carved in the round. They represent the Mourning Madonna, St. Bartholomew and two angels with gilded clothes and polychrome features.  
The stylistic features are late seventeenth-century and the delicate carving is associated with a skilled use of a drill.  
After the suppressions of 1798 that affected all religious companies and brotherhoods by the confiscation of their property, many of these processional items got lost. Thanks to a decree by the viceroy of Italy Eugenio Beauharnais in 1807 which stated for each parish church the presence of just one company of the Holy sacrament many processional crosses were preserved as properties of these companies. This happened in Budrio, where even the name of the company was changed.
44cf7449-7064-5e7b-8625-27f3fafdff19.short_description:
This solemn gilded cross bears a rich decoration with vine leaves and vine-shoots made with the drill. It is interspersed with angels carved in the round holding the instruments of the Passion of Christ.  
In the middle is the dead Christ surrounded by the Mourning Madonna, St. Bartholomew and two angels.  
The elaborate design is reminiscent of the local artistic taste of the end of the seventeenth century.

468acf50-7258-56d8-a713-cf291d79a2d6.name: Pilgrimage Church of the Scourged Saviour, Dyje
468acf50-7258-56d8-a713-cf291d79a2d6.alternate_name: Church of St. John of Nepomuk, Dyje (Milfroň, Mülfraun)
468acf50-7258-56d8-a713-cf291d79a2d6.description: The austere single-nave building is typical of the architecture in the Danube Basin during the second half of the 18th century. It poses a contrast to the colourful, mystical and complex paintings for which a printed programme has survived probably put together by the artist himself. Individual sections represent the scenes Ecce Homo, Adoration of the Shepherds, Allegory of Salvation and Allegory of the Church.
468acf50-7258-56d8-a713-cf291d79a2d6.short_description: This pilgrimage church was part of a broad residential network attached to a major Premonstratensian Monastery in Znojmo-Louka. When the monastery was dissolved, the church became increasingly dilapidated. After the displacement of the Czech-German population in 1945 and the sealing of the Czech-Austrian border, the church, situated in the border region, lost its importance. Restoration of the church only began in 2004 as part of the international project, Culture 2000. The paintings with their intricate iconographic programme are by F. A. Maulbertsch and his closest associates.
468acf50-7258-56d8-a713-cf291d79a2d6.method_for_datation: The chronogram in Abbot Lambeck’s consecration inscription over the entrance vault gives the year 1774. A record gives the date of the church’s consecration as 6 September 1778. In addition, the progress of the building work is recorded in correspondence between the abbot of the Premonstratensian Monastery in Louka and the Bishop of Győr, where Maulbertsch also worked at the time.

468acf50-7258-56d8-a713-cf291d79a2d6.history: The pilgrimage church was built after the demolition of the medieval Church of St. Lawrence in a village belonging to the Znojmo-Louka Premonstratensian Monastery. The monastery hospital was located in the village. The Znojmo-Louka Monastery, one of the oldest and richest in the country, created a unique series of buildings and pilgrimage sites in south Moravia associated with the main religious festivals of the year. When the monastery was dissolved by Emperor Joseph II in 1784 the church started to fall into disrepair. It was plundered during the Napoleonic Wars and used as stables and minor repairs did not rectify the structural problems of the building. After the expulsion of the Czech-German population in 1945 and the sealing of the Czech-Austrian border, the church situated in the inaccessible border region, lost its importance. Restoration of the church only began in 2004 as part of the international project, Culture 2000.

482b2fe7-2ab8-521c-aeb6-542db13d4285.name: Chasuble
482b2fe7-2ab8-521c-aeb6-542db13d4285.description:
The background is made of red silk velvet embroidered with different silver threads. The white silver stitches blocking the metallic threads create many different surface motifs of different heights, and flat areas thanks to a light padding.  
Most likely manufactured in Bologna, this vestment has a common decorative scheme especially evident in the chasuble. It is divided in three by a central rich bush of acanthus interlaced with the instruments of the Passion of Christ forming the main decorative feature. Great inflorescences alternate with the crown of thorns, the cock and the glove. They build a sort of central axis from which depart wide branches linked by delicate nets and vine shoots. The vestment is clearly indebted to models made in Rome in the age of Pope Benedict XIV, such as the ones donated to the Cathedral of San Pietro in Bologna. This is evident in the use of the silver thread as a reflective surface. The ample motif extended on a flat surface and the symmetrical disposition of the main shoots lead to Emilian decorative schemes and patterns. The colour red of the vestment and the symbols of the Passion might suggest a use connected with the feast of the Exaltation of the Cross or the Invention of the Cross, the sacrifice of Christ might also be generally referred to martyrdom.  
The high quality of the work was recognized in 1900 when the vestment was sent to the exhibition of sacred art held in Bologna, in the church of San Francesco. In 1926 this same vestment was photographed by the local Soprintendenza in one of the first campaigns documenting church heritage.
482b2fe7-2ab8-521c-aeb6-542db13d4285.short_description: The red background of the chasuble is divided by silver lace in fields. Two leaf garlands curl against a net ground; the sides are marked with a garland pattern in front of a net ground. The central pole springs from an acanthus bush holding the instruments of the Passion of Christ in its spires. Veil, burse, stole and maniple are embroidered using the most decorative patterns from the design.

48f13002-d6a6-5291-8644-79bab6cf36b1.name: Former chapel of St. Ignatius, Bologna
48f13002-d6a6-5291-8644-79bab6cf36b1.alternate_name: The Glory of St. Ignatius; The staircase of the Pinacoteca Nazionale of Bologna
48f13002-d6a6-5291-8644-79bab6cf36b1.description:
The decoration of the chapel of the ex-novitiate of the Jesuits of Bologna, was likely painted around 1675 by the Jesuit painter Francesco Barbieri. It was inspired by the famous illusive decorations painted by Andrea Pozzo. Barbieri, starting from models by Pozzo, develops an illusory architecture that is a sort of prosecution of the real one, typical of the mature baroque language. The work of the Jesuit painter shows a strong ideal basis: the glory of the saint, taken to heaven by the angels, is a clear self-celebration of the powerful religious order founded by him. The monogram of the Jesuits is painted on one of the short sides of the architecture, above an illusive balcony and is lifted by two angels. Barbieri is not Andrea Pozzo and the painting shows less dramatic movement of the figures, and the colours are less vibrant. He lacks the impressionistic touch and the virtuoso movement of his master. Barbieri tends to simplification perhaps because of his young age or his still developing skills. At this time, he is just one of the many careful pupils of a great master.  
A letter of Andrea Pozzo to the Rector of the College of Mondovì shows evidence that there was a real contact between Pozzo and Barbieri. In particular in 1693 for the painted architecture of San Bartolomeo in Modena, Barbieri used Pozzo's *Perspectiva Pictorum et Architectorum* and possibly even some of his drawings. The glory of St. Ignatius painted by Barbieri on the vault of the chapel of the novitiate of Bologna in 1675 is strongly influenced by Pozzo's ceiling decorations.
48f13002-d6a6-5291-8644-79bab6cf36b1.short_description: The chapel was built on the east wing of the Jesuit novitiate in 1660, in 1803 it became part of the Academy of Fine Arts of Bologna and in 1882 was made into the present Pinacoteca Nazionale by Royal decree. The Jesuit Giuseppe Barbieri, a pupil of father Andrea Pozzo, soon decorated the ceiling quoting his master’s Roman frescoes. There are in fact many affinities with the decoration of St. Ignatius in Rome, where Pozzo celebrated the heavenly glory of the saint through a hardy perspective, opened inside an illusive painted architecture.

*Dall'isola alla città: i Gesuiti a Bologna* (eds. G. P. Brizzi and A. M. Matteucci), Bologna, 1988.

48f13002-d6a6-5291-8644-79bab6cf36b1.history:
In the seventeenth-century the Jesuits decided to build a novitiate in Bologna. On the 11th of May in 1627 they bought a whole block of houses in via Belle Arti. In 1660, after long discussions about the utility of a novitiate in Bologna, the work finally started. The chapel of the novitiate of St. Ignatius was created for private worship, especially for the prayers of the novices. In the past its decorations have been attributed to father Pozzo himself, the celebrated Jesuit artist who painted some of the most extraordinary baroque frescoes for his religious order.  
Architect Leone Pancaldi led the refurbishing of the Pinacoteca Nazionale, between 1957 and 1973. At that time the ex-novitiate chapel on the upper floor housed eighteenth-century Bolognese paintings. It was enlarged by breaking the floor and became the museum's main entrance with the stairway leading to the first floor. The original trompe- l’oeil ceiling with the glory of the saint was thus emphasized.

491f0842-76f0-5189-aaa5-0b2d4ba9a6c4.name: Sanctuary of Bom Jesus de Matosinhos
491f0842-76f0-5189-aaa5-0b2d4ba9a6c4.alternate_name: Igreja paroquial de Matosinhos; Igreja do Salvador
491f0842-76f0-5189-aaa5-0b2d4ba9a6c4.description:
Bom Jesus de Matosinhos Church has three naves, a chancel and two side chapels. It was re-built to the plans drawn by Nicolau Nasoni, who was instructed by the brotherhood to renew the church, the earlier version of which dated from the 16th century.  
The reconstruction retained the 16th-century floor plan, arches and columns, but Nasoni added the Baroque façade and partially changed the elevations according to the new taste, thus allowing the installation of a coffered ceiling.  
Several restorations and renovations have endowed the church with a series of gilt wood altarpieces, appropriately scaled to the building, and seen the chancel completely covered with gilt and carved woodwork.
491f0842-76f0-5189-aaa5-0b2d4ba9a6c4.short_description: A church belonging to an ancient pilgrimage sanctuary with three naves and a symmetrical façade of two towers, the latter designed by the Italian Baroque architect, Nicolau Nasoni.
491f0842-76f0-5189-aaa5-0b2d4ba9a6c4.bibliography:
Brandão, D. P., *A obra de Nicolau Nasoni no actual Concelho de Matosinhos*, Porto, 1964.  
Oliveira, M. J., *Matosinhos* (…), 1989.
491f0842-76f0-5189-aaa5-0b2d4ba9a6c4.history: The origin of the sanctuary is linked to a legend which, similar to other Portuguese legends, has its mythical origins in an object of worship. According to legend, the wooden figure of the Senhor de Matosinhos (Our Lord of Matosinhos) was thrown into the sea by Nicodemos in Palestine. The figure was found in Espinheiro, Matosinhos, on 3 May 124. During the journey it had lost an arm but no one was able to repair it. Later, an old woman was surprised by a dry branch that kept springing out of the fire and recognised it as the figure's missing arm.

4c881754-170e-5cd4-8648-308538d3d9c9.name: *Our Lady of Rosary*
4c881754-170e-5cd4-8648-308538d3d9c9.description: Victory at the Battle of Lepanto was attributed to the Blessed Virgin Mary after a rosary procession was offered on that day, in St. Peter’s Square in Rome, for the success of the mission of the Holy League to hold back Muslim forces from overrunning Western Europe.
4c881754-170e-5cd4-8648-308538d3d9c9.location: Chiesa della Natività di Maria, Portoferraio, Isola d'Elba, Italy

4d1ac747-041e-5297-a029-df8e54693f52.name: Church of St. Barbara
4d1ac747-041e-5297-a029-df8e54693f52.description:
The Church of St. Barbara is an example of folk architecture built of common oak, which grew in nearby woods. The interior originally comprised a simple square with a three-sided apse and a large porch topped by a bell tower. The porch was incorporated into the newly built nave in the first half of the 18th century. The new tower just above the west entrance and the sacristy, were additions of 1876 as was the wooden choir. In 1912, the small, south porch was built.  
The painted interior of the church creates a strong contrast to the brown monochromic exterior. It is completely wood panelled and was painted throughout the 17th and 18th centuries with floral and figurative motives. On the upper panels of the side-walls are painted saints and martyrs (*St. Andrew the Apostle*, *St. George Slaying the Dragon*, *St. John of Nepomuk*, *St. Apolonia*, *St. Peter*, *St. Frances Xavier*, *St. Mary Magdalene*, *St. Agnes*, the *Evangelists,* the *Immaculate Conception,* *Christ on the Cross*, *St. Kümernissa* and *St. Mary the Protector*). Among these are scenes from the Life of St. Barbara. The main altar dates to the late 17th century but it is still in the form of a Late Gothic winged retable decorated with cartilage ornaments. Both the central altarpiece and the painting above it represent the saint and martyr, St. Barbara, one of north Croatia's most popular saints. Four paintings of the Life of St. Barbara are on the open wings, while on the closed wings and outer fixed parts of the retable there are eight scenes from the Passion of Christ. There are also two side altars, one dedicated to St. Anne (the Holy Family) and the other to the Ascension.  
Among the rest of the inventory there are four Roman Missals dating from 1712, all printed in Venice, and the final one by Elisabetta Picicni (Venice, 1648–1734), a well-known graphic artist and member of the Franciscan Order.
4d1ac747-041e-5297-a029-df8e54693f52.short_description: The Church of St. Barbara is the best-known “representative” of wooden Baroque architecture in North Croatia. Small and modest, it stands today in the middle of a field in Velika Mlaka, not far from Zagreb. Wooden churches were a typical feature of the landscape of North Croatia in the 17th and 18th centuries because building in wood was not expensive and, furthermore, there was no need to employ an architect, as craftsmen with some knowledge of building houses could do the job. These churches, still preserved in some villages, are distinguishable from secular houses of the time only by a bell tower and simple, one “nave” interior. For the poor peasants of the region it was the only way to have a church in each village.

Laszowski, E., *Povijest plem. Općine Turopolja*, Zagreb, 1911.  
*Kapela sv. Barbare u Velikoj Mlaki*, (ed) Sanja Cvetnić.,,Zagreb, 2008.  
Cvitanović, D., ''Turopoljske ljepotice'' in *Kaj, časopis za kulturu i prosvjetu*, Zagreb, year 7, 5–6, 1974., pp. 65–104.  
*Kapela sv. Barbare u Velikoj Mlaki*, Cvetnić, S., (ed.), Zagreb, 2008.
4d1ac747-041e-5297-a029-df8e54693f52.history: Velika Mlaka was once the centre of the Noble District of Turopolje. The church itself, built in the middle of the 18th century as a graveyard chapel, belonged to the Parish in Odra. Archival sources, the so-called *Canonic Visitations*, first mention the Church of St. Barbara in 1692, but the fact that the bell in the bell-tower was produced in Graz in 1642, indicates that the church itself was built in the first half of the 18th century. In 1976, it became the parish church.

51e979e1-5041-52d1-b9e1-0d200f1af77f.name: Monstrance from Kopřivná
51e979e1-5041-52d1-b9e1-0d200f1af77f.description:
The pedestal of this monstrance, with its relief and shell-like ornamentation, is decorated with angels’ heads, their eyes turned to heaven. The stem is a simply rendered figure of the Virgin Mary standing on a crescent moon and globe, encircled by a serpent. The spiral kinesis is enhanced by the modelling of clouds, corn stalks and grapes on a casket crowned with the figure of God the Father and an angel adoring a cross decorated with red glass.  
The uniquely shaped monstrance with the Virgin Mary Immaculata was designed by Franz Ignaz Günther as part of his decoration of the Church of the Holy Trinity in Kopřivná. The church was built by Jan Ludvík of Žerotín-Lilgenau on the border between north Moravia and Silesia as a memorial pilgrimage site. The monstrance was made to fit the high altar tabernacle, below Günther’s statue of the Immaculata.  
The composition drew on Günther’s design of a copper monstrance for Munich, as well as on Egid Quirin Asam’s design of a monstrance for the Church of St. John of Nepomuk, also in Munich. All of these were preceded by a diamond monstrance in the Loretto, Prague, which was made in Vienna and designed by Johann Bernard Fischer of Erlach.  
The silversmith who executed the design participated in the creation of the Holy Trinity Column, Olomouc and the tomb of Olomouc Bishop Schrattenbach (Kroměříž, Church of St. Mauritz). Günther arrived in Olomouc after journeyman service in Augsburg, Nuremberg, Frankfurt, Linz and Vienna and worked for the Count of Žerotín. In 1757 he studied at the Vienna Academy in Munich, where he settled, becoming one of the most influential Bavarian sculptors of the 18th century.  
During the Baroque period, the monstrance became a decorative object worthy of adoration, apart from its practical use of carrying the Holy Communion.
51e979e1-5041-52d1-b9e1-0d200f1af77f.short_description: A uniquely shaped monstrance with the Virgin Mary Immaculata it was created in an Olomouc metal workshop to the design of later famous Munich sculptor, Franz Ignaz Günther. It was part of his overall decoration for the Church of the Holy Trinity in Kopřivná, on the border between north Moravia and Silesia.
51e979e1-5041-52d1-b9e1-0d200f1af77f.owner: Roman Catholic Parish of Hanušovice u Šumperka
51e979e1-5041-52d1-b9e1-0d200f1af77f.method_for_datation: The monstrance is marked with three hallmarks one of which is the master’s mark of Simon Forstner.

52a775fc-69c1-5e13-ba25-65aeb14918dd.name: St. Jacob’s Cathedral
52a775fc-69c1-5e13-ba25-65aeb14918dd.alternate_name: Catholic Provost Parish Church of St. Jacob the Elder
52a775fc-69c1-5e13-ba25-65aeb14918dd.description: The church is a cross shaped longitudinal building with a succession of four spatial units with shallow dome vaulting. The nave with two horizontal oval dome bays is followed by the crossing, also in horizontal oval form, to which transept-like side apses are appended, the choir is quadratic. The spatial impression is largely formed by the sequence of dome bays in the Venetian tradition. Massive pilasters form the supporting structure and determine the spatial prospect, at the centre of which is situated the high altar with the miraculous picture *Mariahilf* (Mary Help).
52a775fc-69c1-5e13-ba25-65aeb14918dd.short_description: Innsbruck Cathedral is considered the first major building in Tyrol in the mature Late Baroque style. It is a product of the Füssen school of architecture, conceived by Johann Jakob Herkomer and enriched with new forms by his pupil, Johann Georg Fischer. The stuccowork and frescos were also executed in accordance with contemporary forms by the brothers Asam and are of the highest quality.

Dussler, H., *Der Allgäuer Barockbaumeister Johann Jakob Herkomer*, Kempten 1956.  
Weingartner, J., *Die St. Jakobskirche zu Innsbruck*, 2nd edition, Munich 1956 (= Schnell und Steiner Kunstführer No. 287).  
Sauermost, H. J., *Der Allgäuer Barockbaumeister Johann Georg Fischer*, Augsburg 1969, pp. 27–44.  
Bushart, B., Rupprecht, B., *Cosmas Damian Asam 1686–1739, Leben und Werk*, Munich 1986, pp. 223–6.  
Rupprecht, B., *Die Brüder Asam. Sinn und Sinnlichkeit im bayerischen Barock*, 3rd edition, Regensburg 1987, pp. 124–7.
52a775fc-69c1-5e13-ba25-65aeb14918dd.history: Even before the founding of Innsbruck in 1180 there existed a building on this site. The forerunner of today’s church originates from the High Middle Ages. Earthquake damage meant a new building was required, an undertaking supported by the Provincial Governor Karl Philipp von der Pfalz. Herkomer from Allgau was appointed architect and began work on the building in the year of his death, 1717, which was subsequently completed by his pupil Fischer in 1722. Stucco and frescos were executed by the brothers Asam in 1722/23; the consecration took place on 9 September 1724. Altars and further interior work were added between 1725 and 1732. Bomb damage occurred in 1944 and reconstruction was undertaken between 1949 and 1952. The church was elevated to cathedral status in 1964.

5a5065ff-617c-5f77-81aa-546635c333e8.name: *Saint Charles Borromeo Administers the Sacrament to the Plague-Infected*
5a5065ff-617c-5f77-81aa-546635c333e8.description:
This excellent oil sketch (*bozzetto*) is linked to one of Caspar Franz Sambach's early works, the interior decoration of the parish church in Sloup, Moravia, a grand ensemble of magnificent frescoes and altarpieces, which were completed between 1751 and 1754. The Esztergom *bozzetto*, and a slightly larger and more complete version in Breslau (Wrocław; the Narodowe Museum), were produced for the side altarpiece dedicated to St. Charles Borromeo. The composition follows Pierre Mignard's painting for the high altar of the Church of San Carlo ai Catinari in Rome, probably by way of an intermediary engraving.  
Charles Borromeo, the archbishop of Milan at the time of the great plague of 1576, fought heroically against the epidemic; following his canonisation in 1612, he was accorded reverence similar to that of the medieval plague saints. His cult outside Milan strengthened in Rome at first, and then, through Borromeo family connections in Salzburg, it grew further during the reign of Charles VI spreading throughout the Habsburg Empire.  
Born in Breslau (Wrocław), according to local studies, Sambach worked in Vienna from 1740 in the workshop of the sculptor Georg Raphael Donner. He trained as a historical painter at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna, becoming a member in 1759, a professor in 1762 and director in 1773. His fresco and altarpiece paintings were influenced by other Central European painters, the likes of Paul Troger, Michelangelo Unterberger and the younger Franz Anton Maulbertsch. Sambach was a skilful ornamental artist and painted his own architecture; producing the figure inserts that imitate reliefs on his frescoes, as well as on his canvases depicting *putti,* making use of the methods learned from the works of the Austrian, sculptor Georg Raphael Donner. In Hungary, the high altar and ceiling frescoes, together with the altarpieces of the Jesuit church in Székesfehérvár (1749–50), preserve his early, relaxed style. The Esztergom colour sketch, a loose and vivid composition that shows only the lower part of the altarpiece, can be considered as an autograph version (*ricordo*) made by the master.
5a5065ff-617c-5f77-81aa-546635c333e8.short_description: The Silesian, Caspar Franz Sambach, also worked in Hungary (Székesfehérvár, Buda and Nagykanizsa). One of his most important works is the interior decoration in the parish church in Sloup, Moravia, including the altarpiece commemorating Charles Borromeo. Two oil sketches of Charles Borromeo's altarpiece are extant; the one seen here is considered to be an autograph version (*ricordo*) of the Breslau (Wrocław) study.
5a5065ff-617c-5f77-81aa-546635c333e8.provenance: Purchased by Primate János Simor for his Primatial art collection
5a5065ff-617c-5f77-81aa-546635c333e8.obtention: From the Collection of Primate János Simor
